sentences.text: The genus Pendraig contains only one species, Pendraig milnerae, named to honor paleontologist Angela Milner.
This small theropod measured approximately one meter in length when alive.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes an articulated vertebral series and pelvic girdle with missing spines and distal ends, plus a disarticulated left femur from the same individual.
The fossils were recently rediscovered after being stored alongside crocodile bones likely belonging to Terrestrisuchus.
The fossils were originally misidentified as a coelurosaur and later classified as a species of Syntarsus before their true identity was recognized.
The holotype specimen was discovered in 1952 at the Pant-y-ffynnon Quarry in Wales by Kenneth Alexander Kermack and Pamela Lamplugh Robinson.
The fossils were formally named as a new genus of theropod in 2021.
Researchers suggest Pendraig's small size may be due to insular dwarfism, but this is debated because the known specimen is sub-adult.
Spiekman et al. classify Pendraig as a coelophysoid theropod in a polytomy with Powellvenator, Lucianovenator, and the clade containing "Syntarsus" kayentakatae and the family Coelophysidae.
Pendraig lived during the Late Triassic, approximately 215 million years ago in the Norian stage, in what is now Europe.
During the Late Triassic, Pendraig lived in southwestern Britain on islands formed from folded Carboniferous Limestone.
The environment where Pendraig lived consisted of dry forests similar to those found in the Cayman Islands.
